description: We are a team of engineering students from Manisa Celal Bayar University
summary:
Flame-Fall is an interactive atlas of NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments. It answers one question: how much of what NASA has learned about fire in space applies to the places crews will live next?

We took all 24 combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and turned their experiment tables into one consistent dataset of 1,828 test rows. Every value can be traced to its source file and row.

The dashboard places each test on a map of oxygen level against pressure, beside the atmospheres of a spacecraft cabin, a lunar base and a spacesuit. The gap is visible at once: only 20 tests were run inside the lunar-base range, all of them gas flames, and none with the solid materials a habitat is built from.

The atlas also ranks investigations by relevance to a chosen habitat, using a score the user can re-weight; charts measured results such as droplet extinction and burn time; and answers questions in plain language, citing NASA’s documents.

Future habitats will hold more oxygen at lower pressure than the Space Station, and materials burn more readily there. The atlas shows researchers and mission planners what is already known and where the next experiments are needed
details:
What it does

The atlas has four views.

  • Atmosphere map. Every test that records oxygen and pressure (991 of 1,828) is drawn on a chart of oxygen against pressure, beside the atmospheres of a spacecraft cabin, a lunar base and a spacesuit. Filters show prevention, detection, suppression, flame-science or cool-flame research. Selecting a mark opens the investigation’s record, test summary and objectives.
  • Ranking. Each investigation gets a score for a chosen habitat from four parts: how close its tests come to that atmosphere, its fuel type, its fire-safety role, and how much data it has. The user can change the weights, and the order is recalculated on the spot.
  • Test results. Measured outcomes that a map cannot show: how much of a fuel droplet burns before the flame goes out, with and without a suppressant gas, and how long flames burned by fuel.
  • Ask. A question box that answers in plain language and cites its sources. It searches 13,398 passages from 251 NASA documents and records.

How it works

A Python pipeline lists and downloads every combustion investigation from NASA’s PSI repository. Each experiment table has a small hand-written mapping file that says which column feeds which field. No number is typed by hand, and no AI touches a measured value. Two labels per investigation, its fire-safety role and fuel type, are proposed by an AI model that must quote the sentence it relied on; the quote is checked word for word against NASA’s record, and our domain expert reviewed all 48 labels. The dashboard is a static site that reads the resulting files. The Ask service first builds an answer from table rows and quoted passages, then lets an AI model reword it, and discards the AI version if it contains a number that is not in the sources.

What it shows

  • Only 20 tests were run inside the lunar-base range (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less), all gas flames from one experiment. Seventeen more sit within 0.3 psi of it. None used solid fuel.
  • No test was run above 40% oxygen, so the spacesuit atmosphere (100% oxygen at 4.3 psi) is untested.
  • PSI holds no combustion tests in lunar or Martian gravity.

The atlas also states its own limits. Values we had to assume are labelled as assumed, tests that cannot be placed are counted and explained, and 1,278 tests have no recorded outcome in NASA’s tables.

Benefits and goals

Researchers can see which combinations of fuel, oxygen and pressure are untested before proposing an experiment. Safety engineers can find the investigations that apply to a given habitat. Because the pipeline rebuilds everything from PSI, new experiments can be added as NASA publishes them. We hope it helps direct the next fire-safety experiments to where the data is thinnest.

Tools

Python 3.12, Pydantic, PyMuPDF, ChromaDB with the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding model, FastAPI and pytest for the pipeline and Ask service. TypeScript, React, Vite and Plotly.js for the dashboard. GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for deployment, Render for the Ask service. Google Gemini for labelling and answer wording, with NVIDIA NIM as a fallback.
